extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, trial judges, and trial counsel in patent validity/infringement cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when testimony about patent obviousness (and underlying technical questions) may be admitted at trial, including the distinction between expert and lay testimony, applicable disclosure rules, and when evidentiary error requires a new trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony under Federal Rule of Evidence 702
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness who is qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion if the expert's specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or determine a fact in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule 'precisely describes testimony which would pertain to an obviousness invalidity challenge in a patent trial.' It is often helpful to have a technical expert explain the scope of the prior art or motivations for combining components. Expert testimony is appropriate for explaining issues analyzed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on unqualified witnesses offering expert opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an abuse of discretion to permit a witness to testify as an expert on noninfringement or invalidity unless that witness is qualified as an expert in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A witness who is not 'qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education' cannot 'assist the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue.' Courts must exclude opinion testimony on technical issues (including ultimate conclusions) from unqualified witnesses. See Sundance precedent quoted in opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay-witness testimony must not opine on obviousness or underlying technical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from a lay witness that expresses an opinion that a claimed modification 'would be obvious' or otherwise reaches the ultimate obviousness conclusion is inadmissible if it addresses the central legal and technical question of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper lay testimony include answers like 'Yes, I did' to 'Did you think modifying the Cornette system to support two circuits to be obvious?' and similar statements about what would be obvious. Such testimony is 'in the clear purview of experts' and therefore improper from lay witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of technical questions reserved for experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying technical questions related to obviousness that require expert qualifications include: the nature of the claimed invention; the scope and content of the prior art; differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and the motivation of a person of ordinary skill in the art to combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unqualified witnesses may not testify as to these underlying technical matters or the ultimate conclusions derived from them. Admission of such testimony is improper under controlling precedent (Sundance) and Fed. R. Evid. 702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert disclosure requirements under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties offering expert testimony must disclose experts and produce written reports that contain all opinions, reasons and bases for those opinions, and all facts relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose an expert (or to provide required reports) deprives the opposing party of the procedures for testing and challenging the opinion (e.g., depositions, Daubert challenges) and can be substantially prejudicial. The opinion notes that Mr. Piebes was not disclosed as an expert and no such report was provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daubert reliability and expert discovery protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert opinions are subject to Daubert scrutiny for reliability and the expert-discovery rules are designed to allow both sides to prepare and to prevent surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because expert testimony on ultimate issues can significantly impact a jury's decision, courts should ensure reliability and that the opposing party has had the opportunity to test the opinions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2) and (e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting jury instructions may be insufficient to cure admission error
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's limiting instruction does not necessarily cure the prejudice caused by admitting improper expert-like testimony from an unqualified witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An instruction that 'a witness such as Mr. Piebes certainly can ... explain ... what he thinks would occur to him' and that obviousness is 'for you [the jury] to decide' can improperly suggest the jury may consider the lay witness's views on underlying technical questions. Such instructions can permit jurors to rely on the unqualified testimony and thus fail to cure substantial prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for granting a new trial based on evidentiary error (Eleventh Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidentiary errors require a new trial where the error has caused substantial prejudice to the affected party, affected the party's substantial rights, or resulted in substantial injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited standard: Peat, Inc. v. Vanguard Research, Inc. (378 F.3d 1154, 1162). When the jury returns a verdict (e.g., obviousness) it may be impossible to know whether improper testimony provided some or all of the basis for that decision—supporting a finding of substantial prejudice and the need for a new trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standard for denial of new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of a new trial is reviewed under the regional circuit law; in the Eleventh Circuit, such denials are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit applies the appropriate regional-circuit standard when reviewing a district court's denial of a new trial (citing Wordtech). An abuse of discretion finding supports reversal and remand for a new trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analyzed from perspective of a person of ordinary skill (KSR principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness and its underlying components are analyzed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because obviousness is assessed from a POSITA's viewpoint, expert testimony is often necessary to explain what a POSITA would understand from the prior art and whether motivations to combine references exist (KSR Int'l Co. v. Teleflex Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's post-trial independent analysis does not substitute for jury's role
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's decision on a motion for judgment as a matter of law after a jury verdict is not an independent inquiry that converts a jury verdict into a bench trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellee argument that any error was harmless because the court independently decided obviousness is incorrect; obviousness may be properly submitted to and decided by a jury, and JMOL review does not convert the proceeding into a bench trial.
